The Reading Strategies title fits reading comprehension. The formula-before-example requirement is assigned to mathematics and quantitative science, not this reading lesson. Even so, Core Concept teaches counting symbols and multiplying by five before examples 6 and 7 use that conversion; their differences are ordinary count comparisons.

Examples cover behavior inference, selecting supported claims, rejecting an unsupported character judgment, combining clues, testing a necessary assumption, chart comparison, combining a chart with a threshold note, and Filipino inference/main idea/evaluation. Chart-only and chart-plus-note cases require distinct reasoning. The progression adds argument, visual, and qualified-judgment demands beyond the opening behavior case.

All ten examples have Solution labels and numbered reasoning. Examples 6 and 7 display their multiplications and subtraction separately. The other solutions expose the relevant clues and limits before concluding; no essential reasoning step is omitted.
Each display equation in examples 6 and 7 is a single short multiplication or subtraction, such as 6 times 5 equals 30 and 30 minus 15 equals 15. These are narrow enough for a phone.
The teaching paragraphs contain one to three short sentences, with no extended bullet lists. Example extracts and numbered explanations remain in short blocks.

Each of examples 6 and 7 includes a one-line graph specification with title, axis label, zero origin, step size, and all three day values. Example 7 adds its own threshold marker. The visible labeled square charts and scale statements independently supply the data needed to solve.

Inference, infer, conclusion, evidence, premise, necessary assumption, legend, unit, and scale are explained before use. Filipino hinuha, pangunahing diwa, and paghatol receive meanings before their examples. The specialized trading-volume scenario is replaced with an ordinary work-hours scenario.

Core Concept explains connecting clues, matching claim strength, separating reasons from an argument conclusion, and denying a proposed assumption while keeping facts fixed. It teaches chart-symbol conversion and connecting a written limit to values. Filipino teaching explains combining details and restricting judgments to the evidence.

The lesson warns against invented causes, possible-but-unsupported claims, mechanically choosing weak wording, confusing a true conclusion with a sound stated argument, treating helpful details as necessary, inferring causes from counts, and generalizing from one result. The assumption example applies denial to the employee-only rule without claiming Lino could never get a badge another way.
